off.p: Yes, people can survive severe inflation, but there is no budgeting trick that can indefinitely compensate for prices rising faster than income. This is an economic problem, not a personal failure. When wages lag behind prices, your actual purchasing power falls. IMF explanation

A phone costing six months’ wages or a car costing fifty months’ wages shows how unaffordable those goods are; it doesn’t, by itself, establish hyperinflation. For survival, the more useful question is: Does your income still cover food, housing, utilities, medicine, and getting to work?
The practical priorities are:

off.li: Plan around essentials at today’s prices. Update that budget frequently. Repair and share things where practical, and postpone major purchases unless they are necessary to earn a living. A car’s fuel and maintenance also matter.

Shorten the time between earning and using money. Ask for more frequent pay and more frequent wage reviews. If you sell goods or services, use short quote-validity periods and price against the cost of replacing your supplies.

Buy predictable necessities ahead when affordable. A modest supply of food that keeps, toiletries, or other essentials can help if prices keep rising. Only buy what you will use, can store safely, and can afford without losing the money needed for rent or emergencies.

Protect whatever savings you have. Keep enough accessible local currency for immediate bills. For money beyond that, investigate lawful, accessible options such as a more stable currency or inflation-linked savings. Fees, withdrawal access, exchange restrictions, and the institution’s reliability matter. Cash savings are especially exposed to inflation; no alternative is risk-free. IMF discussion

Look for income that can adjust with prices. That might mean negotiating pay, changing employers, offering a service whose price you can revise, or working for customers abroad where feasible. Start with opportunities requiring little upfront money.
Share costs and seek support early. Shared housing, pooled transport, cooperative purchases, family support, and available food or utility assistance can keep essentials within reach.

off.p: Be careful with the idea that inflation makes borrowing beneficial. If your wages stay fixed, repayments can still become unaffordable, especially with variable interest rates or debt in a foreign currency.

If essentials already exceed your income, cutting discretionary spending will not close the gap. You need some combination of additional income, assistance, shared costs, or—if feasible—a move to a place with a better balance between earnings and expenses.
Which country are you in, and roughly how much of your monthly income currently goes toward essentials? That would help distinguish the options actually available to you.

on.p: Yes, people can survive very high inflation, but it can require painful changes and outside support. When prices keep rising faster than earnings, purchasing power falls. Budgeting has limits: if income cannot cover essentials, you need additional income, assistance, or a cheaper living arrangement.

Your phone and car examples show how unaffordable those purchases have become. Establishing hyperinflation requires measuring how quickly prices rise over time; the practical problem you describe is serious either way.
A useful order of priorities is:

on.li: Work out what it costs to get through the next week. Price food, housing, utilities, necessary medicine, and transport to work. Update those prices weekly. This tells you whether you have a surplus to protect or a shortfall to address.

Buy planned necessities promptly when prices are rising rapidly. A modest supply of food that keeps well can help if you have safe storage. Keep enough accessible money for bills and emergencies. Bulk purchases only help when you will use them and can still meet other essential expenses.

Seek faster income adjustments. Ask about more frequent pay, regular wage reviews, or transport and meal allowances. If you work for yourself, review prices against current replacement costs and shorten payment deadlines. Consider additional work where the likely earnings justify the time and expenses.

Protect any savings cautiously. Inflation erodes the purchasing power of cash and deposits when their returns lag behind prices. Where legal and accessible, holding some savings in a more stable currency may help, but exchange fees, withdrawal restrictions, and the safety of the provider matter. Keep money for immediate expenses accessible. The IMF describes both inflation’s effect on savings and why households turn to foreign currencies.

Be careful with debt. Avoid borrowing in a foreign currency if your income is in local currency: depreciation can make repayments much harder. Variable interest rates can also rise. Even fixed-rate debt requires payments you can afford today. See the IMF’s explanation of foreign-currency borrowing risks.

Use shared resources and assistance early. Sharing housing, pooling shopping or transport, repairing equipment, and checking eligibility for food or utility assistance can reduce pressure. Protect nutrition and necessary medical care as far as possible.

on.p: For a phone or car, consider whether it preserves or increases your earnings, and include maintenance, fuel, and financing in the cost. Months of salary also understate the saving time because you still have living expenses.
What country and currency are you dealing with, and does your current income still cover your basic monthly expenses?

off.p: Yes—particularly reduced student aid, ongoing costs, and complications when you want to sell your share. The exact consequences depend on the country, your ownership share, any mortgage, and whether you live there or rent it out.
The main pitfalls to check are:

off.li: Student aid and scholarships. Means-tested schemes may count property assets, rental income, or both. You can therefore have little cash available yet qualify for less support. Merit-based scholarships may have different rules. For example, Student Finance England includes rental income in its income assessment. Official guidance.

Taxes at several stages. Check purchase/transfer taxes, annual property or wealth taxes, tax on rent, and capital-gains tax when selling. If your parents pay for your share or give it to you, gift-tax rules may also apply. These are country-specific: Ireland, for example, flags several potential taxes when property is transferred. Irish Revenue.

Losing future first-time-buyer benefits. Even a partial ownership interest can affect eligibility. England and Northern Ireland’s stamp-duty rules, for example, generally exclude people who previously acquired a residential property interest, including through a gift or inheritance. HMRC guidance.

Mortgage exposure. Check whether you would be an owner, borrower, guarantor, or some combination. If the loan makes borrowers jointly and severally liable, the lender can pursue you for the whole outstanding debt—not just your ownership percentage. Existing borrowing can also affect your ability to finance your own home later.

Costs without accessible cash. Repairs, insurance, taxes and mortgage payments still need paying while you study. Selling a minority share may be difficult, so the property may not help with tuition or living expenses.

Family disagreements and exit problems. Agree in writing who can live there, who pays expenses, how rental income is divided, and what happens if someone wants out, dies, or cannot pay. Include a valuation and buyout process.

A substantial property share could therefore affect eligibility. England’s student-finance assessment includes rental income. German asset rules, debt deductions, allowances, English income rules.
